items.title: El Niño returns roughly every 2-7 years
items.claim: What is the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)?

options.text: A single tropical storm in the Pacific
A coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Pacific recurring every 2-7 years; El Niño (warm central/eastern Pacific) and La Niña (cool) reshape global rainfall, drought and storm patterns
An annual cycle in the Arctic

items.reveal:
El Niño: weakened or reversed trade winds, warming of central and eastern equatorial Pacific, shifted convection. Typical effects: drought in Australia, Indonesia, parts of southern Africa; floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador; weaker Atlantic hurricane season; warmer global average.

La Niña: the opposite. The 1997-98 El Niño was among the strongest; 2015-16 contributed to record warm years and Great Barrier Reef bleaching.

Gilbert Walker first identified the Southern Oscillation atmospheric pattern in 1924 working with Indian Meteorological Department records. Jacob Bjerknes (1969) linked the atmospheric and oceanic components.
items.why: Global weather has oscillatory components. Forecasts months ahead are skilful when the ENSO state is known — and crops, water supplies and disaster planning across multiple continents depend on the call.

items.title: Antarctica is governed by an international treaty

options.text: It is divided into national territories
The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze territorial claims, demilitarised the continent and committed it to scientific cooperation; 56 countries are now parties
It is divided between Argentina and Chile

items.reveal:
The original 12 signatories (1959) included the US, USSR, UK, Australia, France, Argentina and Chile. The treaty entered force in 1961. The Protocol on Environmental Protection (Madrid Protocol, 1991, in force 1998) prohibits mineral extraction.

Seven countries maintain dormant territorial claims (UK, Norway, France, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, Chile). The US and Russia reserve the right to claim. Treaty parties operate around 70 year-round research stations.

The treaty is one of the most successful international agreements of the Cold War era — both superpowers wanted the demilitarisation to apply to the other.
items.why: Some territory remains explicitly outside the state system. Antarctica's governance shows what's possible when no major power has a strong sovereignty claim — but also illustrates how fragile such arrangements may be as resource interests grow.

items.title: The boreal forest is the world's largest terrestrial biome
items.claim: Which is the world's largest forest biome?

options.text: The boreal forest (taiga) — a circumpolar belt across Russia, Canada, Alaska and Scandinavia totalling around 1.5 billion hectares; larger than all tropical rainforests combined and storing more carbon

items.reveal:
Boreal forest covers around 30% of all forest area and stores an estimated 30-40% of terrestrial carbon — much of it in deep peat and permafrost soils. Russia's taiga alone is around 12 million km².

Dominant species: spruce, fir, pine, larch, birch. Wildlife: brown bear, lynx, wolverine, capercaillie, moose. Productivity per hectare is lower than the Amazon, but the area is far larger.

Climate change is intensifying boreal wildfires — Siberia 2019-21, Canada 2023 — releasing carbon and potentially turning some boreal regions into net carbon sources. Permafrost thaw could release vast methane and CO₂.
items.why: The Amazon dominates public attention as 'the lungs of the planet'. The boreal forest is larger, stores more carbon, and is increasingly fire-prone — but receives a fraction of the press coverage.
